foods.name: Apple

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked slices, or raw apple grated on the coarse side of a box grater. Both are guideline-issued forms; raw chunks are not.
ageBands.prepMd:
Two routes, pick either.

**Cooked.** Peel, core, and slice. Simmer with a splash of water, or roast
covered, until a slice collapses under a fork — five to fifteen minutes
depending on thickness. Serve as finger-length slices, which is also what NHS
suggests for apple: "slices instead of small chunks." At this age the whole-hand
grasp means the piece is held in a fist with an end sticking out, so the baby
sets the bite size.

**Grated raw.** Peel, then grate on the coarse side of a box grater. The shreds
are soft enough to gum and short enough that no single piece can lodge. Stir
into yogurt or porridge, or offer on a loaded spoon.

The pincer grasp arrives — AAP puts it at most often between 9 and 10 months —
so soft cooked cubes about the size of your thumbnail become pick-up-able. They
must still be cooked soft or grated. A pincer grip does not make a raw apple
cube safe; it just means the baby can now deliver one to their own airway.

Grated raw apple stays useful here and is the easier weekday version.

Still cooked soft or grated raw. Baked apple, apple stirred through oatmeal,
apple sauce, apple in a stew.

Raw apple chunks and raw apple slices thick enough to snap off are the one thing
that does not change at twelve months. AAP's line is four years, not one.

choking.note: AAP names "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" on its choking-hazard list and keeps them off the menu until 4 years of age or older. That restriction is about raw pieces, not about apple — cooked or grated apple is fine from six months.
choking.requiredModification: Never raw chunks. Either cook it until it mashes easily with a fork, or grate it raw. Peel it either way.

foods.backgroundMd:
Apple is one of the few foods in this canon that three separate guideline
bodies name by name — and all three name it as a hazard in its raw form. AAP
lists "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" and says to keep them from
children "until 4 years of age or older." CDC's hazard list says "raw carrots or
apples." NHS covers it in its preparation guidance.

That is not a reason to skip apple. It is a reason to change its form, and
unusually there are **two fixes that guideline bodies actually issue** rather
than one someone extrapolated:

- **Cook it** until you can mash it easily with a fork (CDC and NHS both).
- **Grate it raw** (NHS).

Peel it either way. NHS notes that removing the skin makes food easier to
swallow, and apple skin does not break down under gums.

Nutritionally apple is close to filler: 0.12 mg of iron per 100 g raw, and
cooking destroys nearly all the vitamin C — USDA's cooked, peeled entry gives
0.2 mg per 100 g against 4.6 mg raw. So **cooked apple is not a useful vitamin-C
partner for an iron meal**; use [[mango]], [[green-peas]], or
[[butternut-squash]] for that. Apple's value here is that it is cheap,
year-round, familiar, and takes flavour well alongside things a baby is less
sure about.

No juice before 12 months. Applesauce is fine if it is unsweetened — added
sugars are off the menu under 24 months.

[[pear]] is handled differently because a ripe European pear goes soft;
[[korean-pear]] is handled like apple because it does not.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Raw apple is hard, smooth, and breaks into airway-sized wedges under a bite —
the exact combination that makes it one of the named entries on both the AAP and
CDC lists. A baby who can bite a piece off cannot reliably grind it, and the
piece that comes away is the wrong shape.

Cooking and grating are the two fixes, and they are guideline-issued rather than
inferred. Peeling is the third and applies to both.

Test cooked apple the way you would test any cooked fruit: press a piece between
your fingers. If it holds its shape, it needs longer.

foods.name: Avocado

ageBands.servingNote: Slippery is the whole difficulty. Expect it to squirt out of the fist before it gets anywhere near the mouth.
ageBands.prepMd:
Halve, remove the pit, and cut the flesh into long wedges — roughly the length
of an adult finger, thick enough not to collapse when squeezed. Leaving a
strip of skin along the back gives something dry to hold; the skin itself is
not eaten.

One honest caveat about that shape: AAP's published rule is to cut food for
infants into pieces no larger than one-half inch, and that is the only
dimensional instruction any US body issues. Longer soft-food spears are
widespread practice rather than a guideline instruction, and they rest on the
food yielding under light pressure. If a piece holds its shape when you press
it, it is the wrong piece regardless of its length.

Once your baby picks things up between thumb and forefinger instead of raking
at them, small cubes work and are less frustrating. Keep offering a wedge or
two alongside — biting off a piece is a separate skill from picking one up.

However the rest of the table is eating it: cubed, sliced, mashed on toast,
stirred through other foods. No caveat beyond ripeness.

choking.requiredModification: Use fruit ripe enough to yield to gentle thumb pressure. Underripe avocado is a firm food, not a soft one.

foods.backgroundMd:
One of the few foods that needs no cooking and no softening — a ripe avocado
is already at the texture everything else has to be cooked down to. It appears
on no choking-hazard list, and no primary source restricts it.

Do not think of it as an iron food. At 0.55 mg per 100 g of non-heme iron it
contributes very little, so it belongs alongside the foods doing the real work —
[[beef]], fortified [[oatmeal]], [[lentils]] — rather than instead of them. It is
mostly fat and calories, which at this age is a point in its favour.

Related: [[banana]] is the other no-cook soft food and behaves much the same in
the hand.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Ripeness is the only real variable. A hard avocado is a firm raw food and
should be left to ripen rather than served, which is the same logic CDC
applies to hard raw fruit and vegetables generally.

Some people with latex allergy react to avocado, but no primary infant-feeding
source addresses that, so this record makes no claim about it either way.

foods.name: Banana

ageBands.servingNote: Peel back half the skin and leave the rest on — it is the only dry part of a banana.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel about half the skin down, cut the banana in half across the middle, and
hand over the piece with skin still on the bottom half. Bare banana is
notoriously slippery; the skin is the grip.

If you want it bare, one common trick is to score the peeled banana lengthwise
into thirds so it separates into long spears that hold together better than a
whole one. That is a kitchen technique, not an instruction from anybody.

On size: AAP's published rule is to cut food for infants into pieces no larger
than one-half inch, and that is the only dimensional instruction a US guideline
body issues. Longer soft-food spears are widespread practice rather than
guideline advice, and they depend entirely on the fruit yielding under light
pressure.

Once your baby picks things up between thumb and forefinger rather than raking
at them, small pieces stop being frustrating. Cut into short chunks, or leave
some longer pieces alongside so biting stays in practice.

However the rest of the table is eating it — in chunks, sliced onto oatmeal,
mashed into yoghurt. No caveat beyond ripeness.

choking.requiredModification: Use fruit ripe enough to bruise under light thumb pressure. A firm, underripe banana is a hard food.

foods.backgroundMd:
One of the few foods named by a guideline body for this exact moment: NHS lists
bananas among the fruits to offer from around six months, and AAP names small
pieces of banana as a suitable finger food. No cooking, no softening, no
equipment.

It is not an iron food. At 0.26 mg of non-heme iron per 100 g it is close to
the bottom of anything in this canon, so serve it for what it is — an easy,
familiar carbohydrate that a baby can practise on — and keep the iron work with
meat, fortified cereal, beans, and lentils.

Related: [[avocado]] is the other no-cook soft food and behaves much the same in
the hand.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Ripeness is the whole story. A ripe banana compresses to nothing; a firm,
green-shouldered one behaves like a hard raw fruit and should be left a few days
instead.

You may have been told never to serve banana in rounds. Worth knowing where that
comes from: CDC's rule about round foods is written about grapes, cherries,
berries, tomatoes, hot dogs, and string cheese — **banana is not on that list**,
and no guideline body prohibits banana coins. Ripe banana does not hold a rigid
circular shape the way a grape or a hot-dog slice does, which is the property
the rule is actually about. Cut it however suits your baby's grip.

foods.name: Barley

ageBands.servingNote: Mix fortified barley cereal with breast milk, formula, or water — never cow's milk before 12 months.
ageBands.prepMd:
Fortified infant barley cereal: put a spoonful in a bowl and mix with breast
milk, formula, or water until it is smooth and thick enough to stay on a loaded
spoon. Start thinner and thicken it over the following weeks — that transition
is the point of the food as much as the iron is.

Whole barley is a different job. Pearled barley needs simmering for the better
part of an hour, well past the chewy texture an adult would want, and then
grinding or mashing. CDC's instruction for whole grains is to cook and finely
grind or mash the kernels; a whole cooked barley grain is on the hazard list as
written.

Barley cereal takes other foods well — mashed [[butternut-squash]], puréed
[[spinach]], mashed [[tofu]] — which is a good way to get the vitamin-C pairing
and the iron into the same bowl.

Thicker, lumpier cereal, and this is the age Health Canada flags for it: lumpy
textures should be offered no later than nine months. Cooked-and-mashed pearled
barley folded into the cereal is a natural step up from smooth.

Barley porridge with soft vegetables and a mashed protein is a full meal at this
age, and a spoon the baby holds themselves is worth the mess.

However the household eats it — boribap, barley in a soup or stew, barley
porridge. Keep grains soft and well cooked, and mash or chop through anything
that is still distinctly chewy.

Roasted barley tea (boricha) is a common household drink but it is a drink, and
before twelve months drinks other than breast milk or formula displace what a
baby actually needs. It also carries no nutrition worth counting.

choking.requiredModification: Cook whole barley well past the doneness you would eat yourself, then grind or mash it. CDC lists whole cooked grain kernels as a hazard and says to cook and finely grind or mash them.

foods.backgroundMd:
FDA names barley explicitly as an alternative to rice cereal in its
inorganic-arsenic guidance, and CDC recommends offering a variety of fortified
infant cereals — oat, barley, multi-grain — rather than only rice. That is why
barley is here.

**The wheat and gluten question, stated exactly, because it is routinely
muddled.**

Barley is **not wheat** and is **not one of the nine US major allergens**. It
carries no US allergen labelling requirement, and a child with an IgE wheat
allergy is not, by that fact, allergic to barley.

Barley **is** a gluten-containing grain. FDA's gluten-free rule defines those as
"wheat, rye, barley, and other grains produced by breeding" them, so a food
containing barley cannot be labelled gluten-free.

Put together: **barley is a celiac question, not a wheat-allergy question.** A
child with celiac disease must avoid it. But do not read "not wheat" as "safe
for a wheat-allergic child" and serve it on that basis — if there is a diagnosed
wheat allergy in the picture, that decision belongs with the clinician managing
it, not with a labelling technicality.

**On timing, there is nothing to wait for.** ESPGHAN's position is that gluten
may be introduced at any point between 4 and 12 completed months, and that
timing does not affect the cumulative incidence of celiac disease — a position
its 2024 update maintains. No delay is warranted, and delaying does not prevent
anything.

**Fortification is the entire nutritional story, and the gap is about 36-fold.**
Dry fortified barley infant cereal carries **48.2 mg of iron per 100 g**. Cooked
pearled barley carries 1.33 mg. Hulled barley is 3.6 mg raw and pearled 2.5 mg
raw, both before the dilution of cooking. Against an iron requirement of 11 mg a
day at 7 to 12 months, fortified infant cereal is the single realistic vehicle
short of meat — the 48.2 mg figure is for the dry powder, so what actually
reaches the bowl depends on how thickly you mix it, but the ratio holds.

Added iron absorbs inefficiently, so pair it with a vitamin-C food in the same
meal: [[mango]], [[green-peas]], [[butternut-squash]]. Do not pair it with
[[yogurt]] — dairy calcium inhibits non-heme absorption.

**Prepare it with breast milk, formula, or water. Not cow's milk before 12
months.** USDA's "prepared" barley cereal entry is made up with whole milk,
which is not the preparation to copy at this age.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Whole cooked grain kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list.** Barley grains
are small but firm and slippery, and pearled barley cooked to an adult's
"al dente" is exactly the texture the list is about. Cook it soft, then grind or
mash.

**Gluten, not wheat allergy.** Barley belongs in a conversation about celiac
disease. It does not belong in a wheat-free diet, and it should not be presented
as a safe substitute for a wheat-allergic child without a clinician's say-so.

**Never cow's milk to mix it before 12 months.** Breast milk, formula or water
only. This is about volume of unmodified cow's milk, not about dairy in general
— see [[yogurt]], which is fine from around six months.

foods.name: Beef

ageBands.servingNote: Ground and loosened with its own juices, broth, or a puree — dry mince scatters and is hard to gather.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy ground, or grind it yourself. Brown it through, breaking it up finer than
you would for yourself, then stir in enough of its own juices, unsalted broth,
or a familiar puree that it clumps instead of scattering. Loose dry mince is
genuinely hard for a six-month-old to collect — it goes everywhere and nothing
gets eaten.

Cook ground beef to 160 °F (USDA FSIS). Remove any fat or gristle **before**
cooking rather than picking it out afterwards; that is CDC's instruction and it
is easier that way.

A common alternative at this age is a large, palm-sized patty or a strip of
slow-cooked beef the baby gnaws on without detaching pieces. That is widespread
practice, not a guideline instruction, and it depends on the meat being soft
enough to shred under pressure. If it holds together when you pull at it, it is
the wrong piece.

Same ground form, and now easier — a pincer grasp picks up mince that a whole
hand could only push around. Mixed into [[oatmeal]] or mashed vegetables it goes
down faster than on its own.

Whatever the table is eating, subject to two things. Meat still needs to be soft
and cut small: "tough or large chunks of meat" stays on CDC's hazard list past
the first birthday. And processed beef stays out — hot dogs, sausages, and lunch
meat are excluded twice over, once for sodium and once because CDC's rule for
cylindrical foods is to cut them into short thin strips rather than rounds.

choking.requiredModification: Ground or finely minced, never chunks. Remove fat, skin, and bones before cooking, and cook until it mashes with light pressure.

foods.backgroundMd:
Beef is the clearest example of why the old "food before one is just for fun"
line does not hold. WHO's 2023 complementary feeding guideline recommends
animal-source foods — meat, fish, or eggs — **daily** from six months as a
strong recommendation, and Health Canada and the Canadian Paediatric Society ask
for iron-rich foods from about six months, at least twice a day.

What makes beef different from the plant sources is the *form* of the iron. CDC
classifies the iron in meat, poultry, and fish as heme iron and says plainly
that it is more easily absorbed than the non-heme iron in plants and fortified
cereals. Pan-browned ground beef carries 2.93 mg per 100 g, plus zinc, and
unlike [[lentils]] or [[black-beans]] it does not need a vitamin-C food beside
it — heme absorption is not vitamin-C dependent. Pair it with [[broccoli]] if
you like, but for taste, not chemistry.

CPS names "minced" among suitable forms, which lines up with the hazard list:
ground beef is the guideline-friendliest way to serve it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Two separate things, both real.

**Choking.** Chunks of meat are a named hazard-list entry. Ground, finely
minced, or shredded-to-collapse is the safe form; a cube of steak is not, at any
age in this range.

**Cooking.** Ground beef to 160 °F, whole cuts to 145 °F with a three-minute
rest. Ground meat mixes surface bacteria all the way through, which is why its
target is higher than a steak's — for a baby that margin is not worth trimming.

foods.name: Black beans

ageBands.servingNote: Every bean flattened — a whole cooked bean is a named choking hazard, however soft it feels.
ageBands.prepMd:
Cook from dry until the beans collapse, or use canned. Then flatten every single
bean — press each one between thumb and forefinger, or run a fork or potato
masher through the lot until nothing round is left. Loosen with cooking liquid,
unsalted broth, or a puree so the mash gathers on a spoon.

Bean skins sometimes separate and float free of the mash. No guideline body
instructs removing them; parents who do it are following common practice, not a
rule.

Same mash, now self-fed, and it works well spread on a strip of toast or stirred
into [[oatmeal]]. A pincer grasp can pick up an individual bean, which is exactly
the reason to keep flattening them.

Still flattened. This is the part parents are surprised by: "whole beans" is on
CDC's hazard list without an age qualifier, and a toddler who bolts food is not
obviously safer with a round bean than a nine-month-old. Refried, mashed into
rice, or squashed into a burrito filling all work.

choking.requiredModification: Mash, puree, or flatten every bean between two fingers. Whole beans are a named entry on the CDC/WIC choking-hazard list.

foods.backgroundMd:
A cheap, storable, iron-carrying protein that both NHS and the Canadian
Paediatric Society name for this age — CPS's phrase is "mashed beans, peas or
lentils," and the mashing is not decoration.

The iron is non-heme, 2.10 mg per 100 g cooked, which means absorption depends
on what is on the plate beside it. Black beans contain **zero vitamin C**, so
they are the clearest case in this canon for deliberate pairing: CDC advises
serving non-heme iron with a vitamin-C food and names broccoli among its
vitamin-C foods. **[[broccoli]] with black beans is a pairing CDC's own advice
supports**, not a folk tip. [[lentils]] carry more iron per 100 g if you are
choosing between pulses.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Whole beans are a direct entry on the CDC/WIC choking-hazard list**, alongside
whole grapes and chunks of meat. They are small, round, smooth, and about the
size of an infant airway, and being soft does not change the geometry. Mashing
or flattening is the required modification, not a texture preference.

**Sodium, if you use canned.** Beans cooked from dry are about 1 mg of sodium per
100 g. Canned beans are substantially higher — this record does not publish a
figure because we could not verify one, so read the can. Rinsing canned beans
under running water is common practice for cutting the sodium; it is not
guideline-issued, and a no-salt-added can is the more reliable route.

foods.name: Broccoli

ageBands.servingNote: A cooked floret with a length of stalk left on — the stalk is the handle, the head is the part that gets eaten.
ageBands.prepMd:
Steam or boil florets until the thickest part of the stalk takes a knife with no
resistance — softer than you would serve yourself, softer than "tender-crisp".
Leave each floret attached to two or three centimetres of stalk so there is
something narrow to hold while the bushy head goes in the mouth.

The tree shape is why broccoli works early: the head is easy to gum and the stalk
is a built-in handle. Pieces cut small are harder at this age, not safer — a
baby who cannot pick them up ends up raking a handful in at once.

The length of that stalk is common practice, not a rule from anybody. AAP's
published dimensional guidance is the single instruction to cut food for infants
into pieces no larger than half an inch, and no body issues per-food shapes. What
carries the safety here is the cooking: if the stalk resists, it is not ready,
whatever length it is.

Small soft pieces of head and stalk, picked up between finger and thumb. Keep a
whole floret on the tray too — biting a piece off is a separate skill from
picking one up, and it is worth practising.

However the rest of the table is eating it, as long as it is cooked soft. Raw
broccoli and thick raw stalks stay out.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until the stalk gives with no resistance and the head mashes between two fingers. Raw broccoli is a hard raw vegetable.

foods.backgroundMd:
**Broccoli's job in a baby's diet is not its own iron — it is everybody else's.**
At 64.9 mg of vitamin C per 100 g it is one of the foods CDC names when it
advises pairing non-heme iron sources with vitamin C so more of the iron is
absorbed. Its own 0.67 mg of iron is a rounding error next to that.

So serve it *with* something: [[black-beans]], which contain no vitamin C at all,
or [[lentils]], which carry the most non-heme iron in this batch and only 1.5 mg
of C. Fortified [[oatmeal]] is the same case. Broccoli beside any of those is a
CDC-supported combination rather than a nice idea.

It is also the food NHS puts first by name. NHS recommends starting with the
less-sweet vegetables — "broccoli, cauliflower and spinach" — so that a baby
gets used to a range of flavours before the sweeter foods arrive.

Frozen broccoli is a legitimate substitute with one caveat worth knowing: USDA's
figures put frozen at 40.1 mg of vitamin C against fresh broccoli's 64.9 — about
a 38% drop. Iron is essentially unchanged at 0.61 mg. Frozen is still a good
vitamin-C food; fresh is a better one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Raw broccoli is a hard raw vegetable, the category CDC says usually needs cooking
so it mashes easily. Raw florets, crudités, and slaw are not a form to serve in
this age range.

The stalk is firmer than the head and is what to test — a head that mashes on a
stem that does not is the piece most likely to be swallowed in a lump. Press the
stalk, not the florets.

foods.name: Butternut squash

ageBands.servingNote: Roast rather than boil if you can — it keeps its shape better in a fist.
ageBands.prepMd:
Halve it, scoop the seeds, and roast cut-side down at around 200 °C / 400 °F
until a fork slides in with no resistance — usually 35 to 45 minutes. Steaming
works too but leaves it wetter and harder to hold.

Cut finger-length wedges about as thick as two of your fingers. At this age the
whole-hand grasp means the piece is held in a fist with an end sticking out, so
the baby controls the bite. Small pieces are harder now, not safer — they can't
be picked up and end up scooped by the handful.

Skin on or off is your call. Roasted butternut skin is edible and gives
something to grip; peeled is tidier and NHS notes that removing skin makes food
easier to swallow.

Once the pincer grasp appears — AAP puts that at most often between 9 and 10
months — switch to soft cubes about the size of your thumbnail, keeping a few
larger wedges alongside so biting and tearing stay in practice.

Mashed butternut is also a good carrier for something the baby is less sure
about: iron-rich purées, a spoonful of yogurt, ground meat.

However the rest of the table is eating it — cubed, mashed, in soup, roasted in
wedges. Keep some pieces big enough to bite from rather than only pincer-sized
ones.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a piece smashes with light pressure between thumb and forefinger. Raw squash is a hard vegetable and is not appropriate at any age in this range.

foods.backgroundMd:
A sweet winter squash that roasts to a texture a six-month-old can manage
without any special technique. NHS names squash among the vegetables to start
weaning with, and CDC names squash at the category level.

Treat it as a negligible iron source. USDA's two datasets disagree by roughly
threefold — the legacy cooked entry gives 0.6 mg of iron and 15.1 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g, while the newer Foundation sample gives 0.213 mg and 7.6 mg. The
figure in this record is the higher of the two, and even that is small next to
the 11 mg a day a 7–12 month old needs. Its real job at the table is as a
vitamin-C partner: serve it alongside an iron food such as [[tofu]],
[[green-peas]], or [[barley]] cereal, since vitamin C improves absorption of
plant (non-heme) iron eaten in the same meal.

[[kabocha]] behaves almost identically once cooked, and the prep below applies
to both.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Undercooked squash is firm enough to be a hazard. Test a piece between your own
fingers rather than trusting the timer; if it holds its shape under pressure, it
needs longer.

Home-made vegetable purées, squash included, should be cooled quickly,
refrigerated promptly, and not kept for days.

That advice used to have a formal citation behind it: AAP's 2005 clinical report
on infant methemoglobinemia named well water as the main risk vector, found
little or no risk from commercially prepared US infant food, and noted that
cases from home-prepared vegetable foods kept too long continued to occur.
**AAP retired that report in June 2025**, so it is no longer current guidance
and nothing has replaced it. The storage habit stands on its own merits — cool
it fast, refrigerate it, don't keep it for days — but it is now ordinary food
hygiene rather than a cited recommendation. [[spinach]] covers the whole
argument, including where US and EU advice still differ.

foods.name: Carrot

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked to fork-mashable first. Raw carrot is on two separate choking-hazard lists.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel, cut into batons roughly the length of an adult finger, and steam, boil, or
roast until a fork goes through with no resistance and the piece mashes when you
press it. Undercooked carrot is the failure mode — it looks done, softens on the
outside, and stays firm in the middle. Test the thickest piece, not the thinnest.

That baton length is common practice, not a rule any body issues. AAP's one
published dimension is to cut food for infants into pieces no larger than half an
inch, and everything else about shape and length in circulation — here and
everywhere — is convention. What actually carries the safety is the mash test.

Soft cubes, picked up between finger and thumb. Keep a few longer soft batons on
the tray as well, since biting a piece off is its own skill.

However the family eats cooked carrot — in soups, roasted, mashed, stirred
through rice. Raw carrot is still out; see below.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a fork mashes it with light pressure. Raw carrot — sticks, batons, coins, or shreds — is named by both CDC and AAP and is not appropriate in this age range.

foods.backgroundMd:
Carrot is the most heavily flagged food in this batch, and the reason is narrow:
**raw** carrot is named by name on both US hazard lists — CDC's, which lists
"raw carrots" among hard raw vegetables, and AAP's, which names "raw vegetables
like carrot sticks" among foods to avoid until age four or older. Two bodies
naming the same food is rare.

Cooked carrot is a different food mechanically and is fine. CDC's instruction is
explicit: "Cook hard vegetables and fruits, such as carrots and apples, so you
can easily mash or puree them." That single sentence is the whole record.

Nutritionally it is unremarkable here — 0.34 mg of non-heme iron per 100 g, and
3.6 mg of vitamin C, which is too little to count as the vitamin-C partner for
an iron food. CDC does not list carrots among its vitamin-C foods; use
[[broccoli]] for that job. Serve carrot because it is sweet, cheap, holds its
shape when cooked, and babies like it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Raw carrot is the hazard, and it does not stop being one at twelve months.**
AAP's list of foods to avoid — raw carrot sticks among them — runs to "4 years of
age or older." The concern is a hard food that does not compress meeting an
airway that is still small.

This record allows carrot with a required modification rather than banning it,
because the cooking *is* the modification. If it does not mash under a fork, it
has not been modified yet, and it is still the raw-carrot problem in a warm
disguise.

One place the bodies differ: the Canadian Paediatric Society offers **grating**
as a way to serve raw vegetables, where AAP's list simply keeps raw carrot out
until four. Grated raw carrot is not the same object as a stick — but it is
still hard, and AAP names no exception for it. This app follows the more
cautious of the two and treats cooking as the modification for carrot in this
age range.

**On carrot coins, an honest note.** You will be told never to serve cooked
carrot in rounds. The reasoning is sound — CDC's rule for round foods is to cut
them into small pieces or short thin strips rather than discs, because a disc
can seal an airway. But that rule is written about grapes, cherries, berries,
tomatoes, hot dogs, and string cheese. **Carrot is not named in it.** Cutting
cooked carrot into sticks or half-moons rather than coins is a sensible
extrapolation from a guideline, not an instruction from one — and if the carrot
is cooked soft enough to mash, the shape is much less of the story than the
texture is.

foods.name: Chicken thigh

ageBands.servingNote: Finely chopped and moistened with unsalted broth or the pan juices — chicken dries out faster than beef.
ageBands.prepMd:
Take the skin, fat, and bones off **before** cooking, not after — CDC is
explicit about the order, and it means no bone fragments end up in the finished
meat. Braise, poach, or roast the thigh until it pulls apart with a fork, cook
all poultry to 165 °F (USDA FSIS), then chop it finely and stir in enough
unsalted broth or pan juices that it holds together on a spoon.

Run the chopped meat between your fingers before serving. Thigh meat carries
small tendons and the occasional splinter of bone, and that check takes ten
seconds.

Shredded rather than chopped — long soft strands are easy to pick up with a
pincer grasp and easy to gum apart. Chicken mixed into [[oatmeal]] or mashed
vegetables still travels better than chicken alone.

However the family eats it, still soft and still cut small. "Tough or large
chunks of meat" does not drop off CDC's hazard list at twelve months, and neither
do bones.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin, fat, and bones before cooking, then finely chop or shred. Never chunks, and never a piece with a bone in it.

foods.backgroundMd:
AAP names "well-cooked, finely chopped chicken" as a finger food, and the
Canadian Paediatric Society lists cooked chicken among iron-rich first foods.
That is unusually specific for a guideline body — most of them describe
textures, not dishes — so the form to serve is not a matter of interpretation
here.

The iron is heme iron, the readily absorbed kind, at 1.13 mg per 100 g roasted.
That is well below [[beef]]'s, so if the week's iron is coming from one animal
food, beef does more of the work. Chicken's advantage is that it is cheap,
mild, and goes with everything.

Thigh rather than breast is a texture preference, not a guideline position: dark
meat stays moist through longer cooking, and dry chicken breast is the most
common way a promising meat meal ends up on the floor. Breast is not unsafe —
it just needs more help staying wet.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Bones and chunks are the hazard, and CDC handles both with one instruction:
remove all fat, skin, and bones from poultry before cooking, then cook until it
mashes easily with a fork.

Cook all poultry to 165 °F. Undercooked chicken is a food-safety problem, not
just an unpleasant texture, and an infant is the worst person to test it on — no
pink at the bone, and a thermometer rather than "it looked done".

foods.name: Cucumber

ageBands.servingNote: Peeled, and cut as a narrow baton — never a coin. Grating is the easier alternative and needs no judgement about thickness.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel it. Then cut lengthways into narrow batons — long enough that an end sticks
out of a closed fist, and narrow rather than thick, so that if a piece does come
away it is a sliver and not a chunk. Cutting out the seedy core makes the batons
softer.

If judging thickness feels like guesswork, grate it instead. Grated peeled
cucumber is soft, wet, and short, and it stirs into [[yogurt]] or mixes with
other vegetables without any decision to make.

At this age most of what happens is mouthing and gumming rather than eating, and
that is fine — a cold cucumber baton is a pleasant thing to chew on.

Same form: peeled, narrow batons, or grated. The pincer grasp arriving does not
change the geometry rule, and this is the age at which coins become tempting
because they are easy to pick up. They are the one shape to avoid.

Still peeled and still batons rather than rounds. AAP's round-and-firm line runs
to four years, and cucumber is a firm raw vegetable for the whole of that
period.

Grated cucumber folded through plain yogurt is the easy household version and
works as a side for the whole table.

choking.requiredModification: Never raw coins or rounds. Peel it and cut narrow batons, or grate it. The skin is the specific hazard — it does not break down under gums.

sources.body: NHS — Help your baby enjoy new foods (narrow batons; removing skin)

foods.backgroundMd:
**No AAP or CDC infant food list names cucumber.** NHS covers it, but only
inside its general preparation guidance, in a list of vegetables to cut into
narrow batons. So everything in this record is a category rule applied to
cucumber, not a food-specific ruling anyone issued. That is worth saying out
loud, because the category rule it lands in is strict and the food looks
harmless.

Two category rules apply. AAP's is about geometry: "do not feed children younger
than 4 round, firm food unless it is chopped completely." A raw cucumber round
is exactly that shape — a firm disc, roughly airway-sized, with a smooth rim.
CDC's is about hard raw vegetables generally, the same line that puts raw
carrots on the list.

**The skin is the specific hazard**, and it is what makes cucumber different
from a soft raw fruit. Cucumber flesh is watery and yields; the skin is tough,
does not break down under gums, and holds a bitten piece together as an intact
ring rather than letting it collapse. Peeling removes that.

NHS gives the fixes directly: cut vegetables like carrots, peppers, cucumber and
celery into **narrow batons**; remove the skin, which "makes it easier to
swallow"; or grate it for very young children.

**Nutritionally it contributes nothing to speak of.** A USDA entry for cucumber
could not be verified at the time of writing, so this record publishes no iron
or vitamin C figure at all rather than a plausible-looking guess. Treat it as a
hydration and texture food. If you want iron, that is [[tofu]] or [[barley]]
cereal; if you want a vitamin-C partner, [[mango]] or [[green-peas]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Never coins.** This is the single thing to take from this record. A raw
cucumber round is the geometry AAP explicitly warns about, and it is also the
way almost everyone cuts a cucumber.

**Peel it.** The skin does not break down under gums and holds a bitten piece
together. Peeling is a guideline-issued fix, not a nicety.

**Chilled cucumber for teething is common practice, not guidance.** Nobody
issues it. If you do it, the guideline-issued part is unchanged — peel it, cut a
baton — and the chilling is just comfort. A whole unpeeled chilled cucumber, or
a thick unpeeled spear, is not made safe by being cold.

Pickled cucumber is a different food: high sodium, and not appropriate before 24
months.

foods.name: Egg

ageBands.servingNote: Softly scrambled and well cooked — moist curds, no runny patches.
ageBands.prepMd:
Scramble in a little unsalted butter or oil over low heat and keep going until
there is no wet or glossy egg left — AAP names scrambled egg among suitable
finger foods, and soft moist curds are easy to gum. Hard-boiled works too; mash
the yolk and white together with a little breast milk, formula, or water, since
a dry hard-boiled white is rubbery on its own.

Serve the whole egg rather than the yolk alone — AAP's portion is about 1/3 of
a well-cooked egg, not a third of a yolk, and a yolk-only serving is a smaller
exposure than the one that was studied.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing — that is a
logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you are watching and your clinic
is open. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours. That two-hour window
is also why the familiar "wait three to five days before the next new food" rule
adds nothing diagnostically; it just slows down variety.

Same well-cooked forms in pincer-sized pieces: a thin omelette cut into small
squares, chopped hard-boiled egg, egg stirred into [[oatmeal]]. Keep it in the
rotation at least weekly rather than treating the first serving as done.

However the family eats eggs, with one exception that does not expire at twelve
months: still cooked through. Runny yolks, soft-set custards, homemade
mayonnaise, raw batter, and mousse are all uncooked-egg foods.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/3 of a well-cooked egg — scrambled or hard-boiled and mashed — per AAP's stated portion for keeping egg in a baby's diet.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to egg — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the baby could safely eat.

choking.requiredModification: Serve well cooked and soft — scrambled, or hard-boiled and mashed with a little liquid.

foods.backgroundMd:
Egg is the second-best-evidenced allergen introduction after peanut, and the
evidence carries an unusual condition attached: **the cooking is part of the
intervention.** A 2018 review and meta-analysis found moderate-certainty
evidence that introducing egg between four and six months reduces egg allergy,
with "much better efficacy with using cooked as opposed to raw egg." AAP's
wording is the same direction: well-cooked eggs have been studied and shown to
reduce the risk of egg allergy when fed to infants regularly.

So there is no tension between the allergy advice and the food-safety advice
here — well-cooked egg is both the safe form and the effective one.

Two things from AAP are worth carrying: **about 1/3 of a well-cooked egg** as
the portion, and **at least weekly** as the cadence. Introduction is not the
finish line for allergens; a single taste followed by months of nothing is not
what the trials tested.

Egg is also on CDC's list of heme iron foods, at 1.19 mg per 100 g. That is the
classification, given here as CDC gives it.

Related: [[salmon]] is the other major allergen in this batch and follows the
same medical gate.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cook it fully.** FDA and CDC advise against raw or undercooked egg for
everyone, and children under five are singled out: they are about three times
more likely to be hospitalized with *Salmonella*. Cook eggs until the white and yolk
are firm; egg-containing dishes such as casseroles and custards go to 160 °F
(USDA FSIS).

**The bodies disagree, and you should know it.** NHS permits raw or lightly
cooked hen's eggs for babies *if* the eggs carry the British Lion stamp, a
UK-specific *Salmonella*-control scheme with no US equivalent. FDA and CDC make
no such carve-out. This app follows FDA and CDC: in the US there is no stamp
that makes a runny egg a safe infant food. If you are reading UK guidance
alongside this, that is where the difference comes from — not a disagreement
about babies, but a difference in national egg supply controls.

Choking risk from well-cooked egg is low. A whole hard-boiled egg, or a large
piece of firm white, is a different matter — mash or cut it.

foods.name: Green peas

ageBands.servingNote: Peas roll. Smashed onto a loaded spoon or into a thicker purée, they stay put long enough to reach a mouth.
ageBands.prepMd:
Simmer or steam until a pea flattens when you press it. Then smash them —
against the side of a bowl with a fork, or stirred into a thicker purée such as
[[butternut-squash]] so they have something to hold onto.

Loose peas at this age mostly end up on the floor. That is not a safety problem,
it is a physics one: a whole-hand grasp cannot pick up a sphere. Loading a spoon
and handing it over, or spreading smashed peas on a strip of toast, gets more
into the baby.

The pincer grasp — AAP puts it at most often between 9 and 10 months — is
exactly the tool a pea is shaped for, and picking them up one at a time is good
practice. Many parents keep squashing each pea between finger and thumb first.

Be clear about what that habit is. **No AAP or CDC document names green peas as
a choking hazard.** AAP's rule concerns round *firm* food — "do not feed
children younger than 4 round, firm food unless it is chopped completely" — and
a properly cooked pea is soft, not firm. Smashing is a conservative
extrapolation from that rule rather than an instruction anyone issued. It costs
nothing, so it is a reasonable thing to do; it is not a thing you have failed to
do if you skip it.

Whole, cooked, however the rest of the table is eating them. Mushy peas, peas
stirred through rice, peas in a soup.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a pea crushes under light pressure. Smashing each one is a conservative habit, not a rule any guideline body issues — see below.

foods.backgroundMd:
Both CDC and NHS name peas among early vegetables, and they are one of the few
foods on this list that pair themselves: 1.54 mg of iron and 14.2 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g cooked, in the same spoonful. Vitamin C improves absorption of plant
(non-heme) iron eaten in the same meal, so the pea does the pairing work that
[[spinach]] or [[tofu]] need a second food for.

Frozen peas are fine and often better than fresh — they are picked and frozen
quickly, and they cook in minutes. Raw peas hold more vitamin C (40 mg per 100 g
against 14.2 cooked) but are firm, so cooking is the trade you make.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The real failure mode is undercooking. A pea straight from the freezer, or one
blanched for thirty seconds, stays firm — that is when AAP's round-and-firm rule
genuinely applies. Cook until they give.

Dried whole peas and split peas are a different food and need cooking to a soft
mash; CDC lists whole beans as a choking hazard, and a hard dried pulse belongs
in that group.

foods.name: Kabocha squash

ageBands.prepMd:
Steam or roast until completely soft, then cut into finger-length wedges about
two fingers thick. Remove the skin for a beginner — kabocha skin stays chewy
even when the flesh is soft, and chewy is the harder texture.
Soft cubes around thumbnail size once the pincer grasp arrives.

Serve it the way the rest of the table eats it — cubed in a soup, mashed as a
side, or roasted in wedges. Skin can stay on now if it's roasted soft.

choking.requiredModification: Steam or roast until a fork meets no resistance; skin removed for beginners.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics
American Academy of Pediatrics

foods.backgroundMd:
Dense, sweet winter squash — 단호박 in Korean, where it's a common early
weaning food, often steamed and mashed thin. Behaves almost identically to
[[sweet-potato]] once cooked, so it's a natural second food if the first went
well: same shapes, same softness test, different flavour.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The raw squash is very hard and needs real force to cut — that firmness is
exactly the hazard, so the softness test matters more here than with a
softer-fleshed vegetable. Press a cooked piece between thumb and forefinger
before serving; if it holds its shape under pressure, cook it longer.

foods.name: Korean pear

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked slices, or grated raw. Waiting for it to ripen does not soften it — this is not a European pear.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Grated.** This is the easier route and the one that suits the fruit. Peel it,
then grate on the coarse side of a box grater. The shreds are short, wet, and
soft enough to gum. Serve on a loaded spoon or stirred into yogurt or porridge.

**Cooked.** Peel, core, slice, and simmer with a splash of water until a slice
collapses under a fork. It takes noticeably longer than an apple — a dense
Korean pear can want fifteen to twenty minutes — so test rather than time it.
Serve as finger-length slices held in the fist with an end sticking out.

The pincer grasp, most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP, means cooked cubes
about the size of your thumbnail can be picked up one at a time. They still have
to be cooked soft. Being able to lift a raw cube is not the same as being able
to chew one.

Grated raw stays the low-effort option, and now that the pincer grip exists a
small pile of shreds is something the baby can manage alone.

Cooked soft or grated raw, still peeled. Raw chunks and raw batons are the part
that does not change at twelve months — AAP's line for raw fruit chunks is four
years.

If the household is eating bae at the end of a meal, grate the toddler's portion
off the same fruit rather than handing over a slice.

choking.note: No guideline body names Korean or Asian pear specifically. It sits inside AAP's "raw fruit chunks" entry, which AAP keeps off the menu until 4 years of age or older, and inside CDC's hard-raw-fruit line. That is category-level coverage, and this record says so rather than implying a food-specific ruling exists.
choking.requiredModification: Treat it as raw apple. Cook until it mashes easily with a fork, or grate it raw. Peel it either way. Ripening will not make raw chunks safe.

foods.backgroundMd:
**No guideline body names Korean or Asian pear.** AAP, CDC, NHS and Health
Canada all cover it only at the category level — hard raw fruit — so everything
below is that category rule applied to this fruit, not a ruling anyone issued
about *Pyrus pyrifolia*. That distinction is worth stating plainly, because the
category rule it lands in is a strict one.

**Do not carry over the logic from [[pear]].** A European pear is safe raw once
it ripens because ripening softens it. A Korean pear does not do that. It stays
crisp and dense at full ripeness — that crunch is the point of the fruit — which
puts it squarely inside AAP's "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" entry
rather than inside NHS's permission for soft ripe fruit. So it inherits the
[[apple]] rules: cook until fork-mashable, or grate raw, peel either way.

**Iron is zero.** Not low — zero, verified in USDA's entry, alongside 3.8 mg of
vitamin C per 100 g. This is a hydration and flavour food. It is very juicy,
mildly sweet, and pleasant on sore gums when grated; it contributes nothing to
the 11 mg of iron a day a 7–12 month old needs, and it is not strong enough on
vitamin C to serve as the partner for an iron meal. Use it for enjoyment and
variety, and get iron from [[tofu]], [[barley]] cereal, or [[green-peas]].

**Two Korean-kitchen forms that are not appropriate for a baby.** Grated bae is
the standard tenderiser in bulgogi and galbi marinades, mixed with soy sauce and
sugar — that combination is high sodium and added sugar, both off the menu under
24 months. And bae juice, or baesuk simmered with honey, runs into three
separate rules: no juice before 12 months, no added sugars before 24, no honey
before 12. Serve the fruit plain.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The specific trap here is that it looks like a pear and is sold as a pear, so it
invites the pear reasoning: wait until it is ripe, then serve it raw. That
reasoning is wrong for this fruit. Ripeness does not soften it, and a ripe
Korean pear cut into cubes is the same hazard as raw apple cubes — hard, smooth,
and breaking into airway-sized pieces under a bite.

Peel it at every age in this range. The skin is tougher than a European pear's
and does not break down under gums.

Serve it plain: no marinade, no juice, no honey.

foods.name: Lentils

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked until they collapse into a puree — red and split lentils get there on their own.
ageBands.prepMd:
Rinse, then simmer in unsalted water or broth until they lose their shape
entirely. Red and split lentils fall apart on their own in about twenty minutes;
brown, green, and Puy lentils hold together much longer and need either more
time or a mash at the end.

Serve as a thick puree off a loaded spoon, or spread on a strip of toast. No
salt — high-sodium foods are advised against under two years.

Thicker and lumpier is fine now, and lentils are a good carrier for iron-rich
company: stir in finely chopped [[chicken-thigh]] or mix with [[oatmeal]]. Mash
any lentils that are still visibly whole.

However the family eats them — dal, soup, stirred through rice. Softness is
still the test.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until the lentils break down, and mash any that still hold a round shape.

Canadian Paediatric Society
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — iron

foods.backgroundMd:
**The highest non-heme iron of any whole food in this batch — 3.33 mg per 100 g
cooked**, plus 9.02 g of protein, from something that costs almost nothing and
cooks in half an hour without soaking. Both NHS and the Canadian Paediatric
Society name lentils for this age.

Non-heme iron is absorbed less readily than the heme iron in [[beef]] or
[[salmon]], and CDC's answer is to serve it with a vitamin-C food. Lentils bring
only 1.5 mg of vitamin C themselves, so pair them — [[broccoli]] is one CDC
names by name. A dal with a green vegetable stirred through it is doing real
nutritional work, not just filling a bowl.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Here is an honest ambiguity rather than a resolved rule. **Lentils are not
individually named on CDC's choking-hazard list, but "whole beans" is**, and
lentils are pulses. Nobody has published a ruling on whether a cooked lentil
falls inside that entry.

What is clear is the physical difference: a cooked black bean stays a smooth
round object, while a cooked red or split lentil has usually already
disintegrated. This record treats lentils as needing modification — cook them
down, mash what is left round — which costs nothing and stays on the right side
of an entry that may or may not include them. Whole firm lentils, the kind that
survive a salad, are the form to avoid.

No salt, for the same reason as everywhere else in the first two years. Lentils
are not one of the nine major US allergens.

foods.name: Mango

ageBands.servingNote: Ripe mango is slippery. Leaving a strip of peel at the gripping end helps — but the peel is not the part to eat.
ageBands.prepMd:
Pick a mango that gives under gentle pressure and smells sweet at the stem end.
Peel it, cut the two cheeks off either side of the flat stone, then cut
finger-length strips.

Ripe mango is genuinely slippery, which is the main practical problem at this
age. Two things that help: leave a band of peel at one end as a handle while
keeping the eating end bare, or roll the strip in a little infant cereal or
ground oats for grip. Neither is a safety measure — they are grip aids.

An underripe mango is firm. Do not serve that raw in strips: cook it soft or
grate it, exactly as with raw [[apple]].

With the pincer grasp — most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP — soft mango
cubes about the size of your thumbnail work well, with a couple of larger strips
alongside so biting stays in practice.

Mashed mango is also a good carrier for something less popular: stirred into
plain [[yogurt]], or over [[barley]] cereal.

However the rest of the table is eating it, peeled and stoned. Cubes, strips,
blended into a lassi with plain yogurt and no added sugar.

choking.requiredModification: Peel it and remove the stone. Use a ripe mango — an underripe one is firm and needs cooking or grating like raw apple.

foods.backgroundMd:
A ripe mango is about as easy as first foods get: soft, sweet, and mashable
without cooking. Neither AAP nor CDC names mango individually — NHS covers it at
the category level as a soft ripe fruit — so its place here is category-level
coverage rather than a food-specific ruling.

**Vitamin C varies by cultivar by roughly fivefold**, so this record gives a
range rather than a number: USDA's verified entries run from **25.5 mg per 100 g
for Tommy Atkins to 168 mg for Ataulfo**, with the generic entry at 36.4 mg. Any
of those makes mango a genuinely useful vitamin-C partner for a plant-iron meal
— [[tofu]], [[green-peas]], [[barley]] cereal — since vitamin C improves
absorption of non-heme iron eaten alongside it. Mango's own iron is a trace
0.16 mg per 100 g, and the two Foundation cultivar samples measured zero.

Peel it and take the stone out. NHS's instruction is to always remove hard pips
or stones, and a mango stone is large, fibrous, and exactly the wrong shape.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The stone is the hazard, and it is the only one that comes with an actual
guideline instruction: remove hard pips and stones. Do not hand over a gnawed
stone as a teether — it is the wrong size and shape, and the fibres come away.

**Skin contact, not food allergy.** Mango peel, leaves and stem contain
urushiol-family compounds — the same chemical family as poison ivy — and
peer-reviewed dermatology literature documents type-IV *contact* dermatitis on
the lips and face in people already sensitised to poison ivy or oak. Two things
about that. First, it is not a food allergy and not an IgE reaction; it is a
delayed rash from touching the peel. Second, prior sensitisation is very
unlikely in an infant who has never met poison ivy. This is peer-reviewed
literature, **not** a pediatric guideline, and no body issues advice about it.

The practical consequence is small and you were going to do it anyway: serve
peeled flesh, and keep the peel off the tray.

foods.name: Oatmeal (fortified infant oat cereal)

ageBands.servingNote: Mixed with breast milk, formula, or water until it is smooth and drops off the spoon.
ageBands.prepMd:
Follow the box, then follow CDC: mix the cereal with breast milk, formula, or
water until it is smooth. Start thin — closer to a pourable consistency than a
paste — and thicken it over the following weeks as your baby gets better at
moving food to the back of the mouth.

Load the spoon and hand it over, or let them take it off a loaded spoon you hold.
Either way most of the first weeks land on the tray and the chin. That is the
job at this age.

Thicker, and increasingly self-fed. This is also the point where oatmeal earns
its keep as a carrier: mashed [[black-beans]], flaked [[salmon]], or fruit stir
into it and go down easily.

However the family eats it. If you have moved to rolled or steel-cut oats cooked
from scratch, keep the smoothness rule in view — CDC's instruction is to cook and
then finely grind or mash whole-grain kernels, and steel-cut oats are kernels.

choking.requiredModification: Serve as a smooth porridge. Whole or steel-cut grain kernels must be cooked and then finely ground or mashed — whole cooked kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list.

foods.backgroundMd:
**The fortification is the entire point, and it is easy to lose by accident.**
Fortified infant oat cereal carries 64.1 mg of iron per 100 g dry. Plain oatmeal
cooked in water, unenriched, carries 0.90 mg. That is roughly a seventyfold gap
between two things a parent would reasonably both call "oatmeal".

So: **a pot of homemade porridge is not a nutritional substitute for fortified
infant cereal.** It is a fine food and a fine texture. It is not doing the iron
job, and if it quietly replaces the fortified box, the iron in the diet drops by
almost all of it. If you prefer cooking your own oats, keep an iron-rich food
somewhere else in the day — see [[beef]] or [[lentils]].

The iron in fortified cereal is added, non-heme iron, not the heme iron in meat.
CDC's advice to serve a vitamin-C food alongside non-heme iron applies here:
[[broccoli]] is one CDC names by name.

**Why oat rather than rice.** CDC's own wording is to "offer a variety of
fortified infant cereals such as oat, barley, and multi-grain instead of only
rice cereal," and AAP notes rice cereal does not have to be the first cereal.
The concern behind that is inorganic arsenic, which concentrates in rice: FDA
has set an
action level of 100 ppb for infant rice cereal and notes that infants' rice
intake relative to body weight is about three times an adult's. Oat sidesteps
that without giving anything up.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Smooth porridge is a low-risk texture. **Whole cooked grain kernels are not** —
they are a named entry on CDC's choking-hazard list, and CDC's instruction is to
cook and then finely grind or mash them. Instant and quick oats break down on
their own; steel-cut and whole groats do not, so blend or mash those.

Oats are not one of the nine major US allergens. Oat products are sometimes
processed on shared lines with wheat, but no infant-feeding guideline addresses
that question, so this record makes no claim about it in either direction — if
wheat matters in your household, read the label.

foods.name: Peanut

ageBands.servingNote: Thinned to the consistency of a runny yoghurt — never a spoonful or a thick glob.
ageBands.prepMd:
Stir about 1/4 teaspoon of smooth peanut butter into warm water, breast milk,
formula, or a puree the baby already eats, until it's thin enough to pour off
a spoon. Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you're not rushing —
that's a logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you're watching, and
your clinic is open.

Watch for about two hours. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours,
which is also why the familiar "wait 3–5 days before the next new food" rule
adds nothing diagnostically — it just slows down variety.

Same thinned form. Thickness, not quantity, is the hazard here: nut butter
stiff enough to hold its shape can obstruct an airway.

Still thinned or spread thinly — on a strip of toast, stirred into oatmeal or
yoghurt. The maintenance target doesn't change: keep it in the rotation at
least three times a week rather than letting weeks lapse.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of smooth peanut butter thinned with warm water, breast milk, or formula, stirred into a familiar puree.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an egg allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first peanut exposure — that group may need testing and a supervised introduction between 4 and 6 months (NIAID 2017 addendum, Tier 1). Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in infants without symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance.

choking.note: Whole peanuts are a high-risk choking hazard and are not appropriate before age 4.
choking.requiredModification: Never whole nuts and never a spoonful or thick glob of nut butter — thin it, or spread it very thinly.

sources.body: NIAID (Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy, 2017)
LEAP trial (NEJM 2015)
CSACI — "early introduction is not enough" position statement
American Academy of Pediatrics

foods.backgroundMd:
The single most consequential food on this list. The LEAP trial randomized
infants at high risk to eat peanut or avoid it, and early, sustained
introduction reduced peanut allergy by roughly 81%. That result is why the
old "delay allergens" advice was reversed.

The part that gets lost: **introduction is not the finish line.** LEAP's
protocol wasn't a taste, it was about 6 g of peanut protein a week across
three or more feedings, sustained for years. CSACI's position statement is
blunt that occasional exposure may be worse than none — a single taste
followed by months of nothing can raise the risk of sensitization rather than
lower it. So this food has a maintenance schedule, not a checkbox.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Two separate risks, often confused.

**Allergy** is managed by early, regular exposure — with the medical gate
above for babies with severe eczema or egg allergy.

**Choking** is managed by form. Whole peanuts and tree nuts are firm, round,
and airway-sized: AAP keeps them off the list until age 4. A spoonful of thick
peanut butter is on the same list. Thinned or spread very thinly, peanut is
fine from six months.

foods.name: Pear

ageBands.servingNote: Ripeness is the whole decision. Press the flesh near the stem with your thumb — if it gives, it can go raw and peeled.
ageBands.prepMd:
Check ripeness first. Press the flesh just below the stem with your thumb. If it
yields, it is ripe.

**Ripe:** peel it, quarter it, remove the core, and cut finger-length slices.
The whole-hand grasp means the baby holds the slice in a fist and bites the
protruding end. Ripe pear is slippery once peeled — leaving a small band of skin
at the gripping end gives some purchase, but the eating end should be peeled.

**Firm:** peel, core, and simmer or roast until a slice collapses under a fork,
then serve the same way. Grating raw works too and needs no pan.

With the pincer grasp — most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP — soft ripe pear
cut into thumbnail-sized cubes is easy to pick up, and peeled. Firm pear still
gets cooked or grated first; the pincer grip changes what the baby can lift, not
what they can chew.

However the rest of the table is eating it, provided it is ripe and peeled. Firm
pear still wants cooking or grating.

choking.requiredModification: Judge the ripeness first. A ripe pear that yields to gentle thumb pressure can be served raw, peeled. A firm pear is treated exactly like raw apple — cook it soft or grate it — and peeled either way.

foods.backgroundMd:
Pear is the food on this list where the label on the shelf tells you nothing and
your thumb tells you everything. **Ripeness decides the whole record.**

A ripe European pear — one that gives when you press near the stem — is soft
enough that NHS's permission for soft raw fruit applies directly. Low risk,
peeled, no cooking.

An underripe pear is a hard raw fruit, and everything in [[apple]] applies to it
unchanged: cook until fork-mashable, or grate it raw, peel either way. Pears are
usually sold hard because they travel and store better that way, so most pears
you bring home are in this second category for a few days.

Nutritionally it is a trace contributor — 0.18 mg of iron and 4.3 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g. Serve it because it is soft, sweet, and easy, not because it moves
any number.

One thing this record deliberately does not claim: pear is often described as a
remedy or a trigger for infant constipation because of its sorbitol content. **No
primary-source guideline addresses pear, sorbitol, and infant stool**, so there
is no claim here in either direction. If stooling is a worry, that is a question
for your pediatrician rather than a fruit choice.

See also [[korean-pear]], which looks like a pear and behaves like an apple.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The mistake to avoid is treating "pear" as a single food. A rock-hard pear cut
into cubes is the same hazard shape as raw apple, and the fact that it is a pear
does not change that.

Peel it at every age in this range. Pear skin is thin but does not break down
under gums, and NHS notes that removing skin makes food easier to swallow.

Whole pear halves and long unpeeled wedges thick enough to snap into a chunk are
not appropriate; slices and cubes are.

foods.name: Salmon

ageBands.servingNote: Flaked fine and checked by hand for bones, then moistened so it does not crumble apart.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy it boneless if you can, and go over it with your fingers anyway. Remove the
skin and any bones **before** cooking, which is CDC's instruction and NHS's
("no bones") — pin bones are far easier to find in a raw fillet than in a hot
cooked one.

Bake, poach, or pan-cook until the flesh is opaque all the way through and
flakes apart under a fork. Flake it fine, run the flakes through your fingers
one more time, and moisten with a spoonful of the cooking liquid or a puree so
it holds together instead of powdering.

Deboned salmon flesh is soft and low-risk. The bones are the entire hazard.

Larger flakes, self-fed. Salmon stirred through [[oatmeal]] or mashed vegetables
is easier to gather than dry flakes on a tray.

However the family eats it, still deboned and still cooked through. No raw fish
at this age.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned salmon, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. Note also that NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway should not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove all bones and the skin before cooking, then flake the cooked fish and run it through your fingers to find any bone you missed.

foods.backgroundMd:
Salmon does two jobs at once: it is heme iron at 1.03 mg per 100 g — the readily
absorbed kind, like [[beef]] and [[chicken-thigh]] — and it is the food most
families use to introduce fish, one of the nine major US allergens.

On the allergen side, AAP's position is that there is no evidence delaying fish
past four to six months prevents allergy. The old advice to hold allergens back
was reversed for peanut on trial evidence, and the delay advice for the other
allergens went with it. Fish is introduced like any other food, with the medical
gate above for the babies who need it.

On mercury: FDA and EPA place salmon in the **Best Choices** category, and
within that in the sub-list of fish that are *even lower* in mercury. Among
common fish it is close to the safest choice you can make.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones.** "Bones in meat or fish" is a named entry on CDC's choking-hazard
list. Debone before cooking, then check the cooked flakes by hand. Whole small
fish and bone-in steaks are not a form to serve here.

**Cooking.** Cook salmon through — opaque to the centre, flaking cleanly. No
raw, no smoked, no cured: none of those are cooked, and cured fish is
salt-preserved besides, where high-sodium foods are advised against under two
years. This record does not print a target internal temperature for fish: the
figure in general circulation could not be confirmed against USDA's own chart
while this was written, and we would rather give you the doneness test than a
number we cannot stand behind. Opaque through the middle, flaking cleanly under
a fork — that is what the temperature describes anyway.

**How much per week — there is no infant answer.** FDA and EPA's fish advice —
two servings a week from Best Choices, at a serving size of about one ounce for
a one-to-three year old — is written for **children ages 1 to 11**. It starts at
the first birthday. **No US body publishes a per-week amount for a six-to-eleven
month old**, so this record does not give one: any specific infant ounce figure
in circulation has been extrapolated by somebody, and we are not going to add
another. Serve salmon as one of several protein foods across the week, and if
you want an actual number for your own baby, ask your pediatrician.

For wild-caught fish from local waters, check your state or provincial
advisories — those are issued per water body and FDA's national list does not
replace them.

foods.name: Spinach

ageBands.servingNote: The risk here is texture, not hardness — cook it and chop it fine so leaves cannot ball up into a wad.
ageBands.prepMd:
Wash it well — spinach carries grit, and grit is the most common actual problem
with it. Wilt it in a pan with a splash of water for two or three minutes until
it collapses, then squeeze out the liquid and **chop it finely**.

Then mix it into something with body: mashed [[butternut-squash]], [[barley]]
cereal, [[tofu]], mashed beans. A pile of loose cooked spinach is hard to pick
up and easy to gather into a wad; carried in a thicker food it goes down easily
and tastes less sharp.

Cook it fresh rather than reheating a batch. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate
them, and serve them cold or not at all.

Same handling — cooked, squeezed, finely chopped, carried in something. The
pincer grasp does not help much with a leaf; what changes is that the baby can
now self-feed a thick spinach-and-grain mixture from a loaded spoon or as small
soft lumps.

A cooked spinach and egg or tofu scramble holds together well enough to pick up,
which is the first form of spinach most babies manage on their own.

However the household eats it, still cooked and chopped rather than served as
whole leaves. Stirred into rice or pasta, in a soup, in sigeumchi namul made
without salt or soy sauce, in a dal.

Raw spinach salad is a different proposition — thin whole leaves are the wad
problem in its purest form — and is better left until well past this range.

choking.requiredModification: Cook it, then chop it finely. A whole cooked leaf is thin and slippery and can gather into a wad — that, not firmness, is the hazard.

frequencyLimit.reason: EFSA advises that a risk cannot be excluded for infants eating more than one spinach meal in a day. One serving a day is well inside that. This is an EU precaution; CDC and the Dietary Guidelines impose no limit at all.
